today_content.sher_roman:
Laayī hayāt aa.e qazā le chalī chale,
apnī ḳhushī na aa.e na apnī ḳhushī chale.

Behtar to hai yahī ki na duniyā se dil lage,
par kyā kareñ jo kaam na be-dil-lagī chale.
today_content.sher_urdu:
لائی حیات آئے قضا لے چلی چلے
اپنی خوشی نہ آئے نہ اپنی خوشی چلے

بہتر تو ہے یہی کہ نہ دنیا سے دل لگے
پر کیا کریں جو کام نہ بے دِل لگی چلے
today_content.english_translation: Life brings, death takes; we neither come nor go by will, yet how can one truly live without a heart's attachment?
today_content.caption:
Who truly controls their own journey? Zauq, the esteemed Ustad of Bahadur Shah Zafar, despite his celebrated status, often penned verses reflecting a deep, almost resigned understanding of human helplessness and the transient nature of life. These lines reveal his mature perspective, perhaps shaped by witnessing the profound shifts and losses in Delhi, expressed with a simplicity that touches universal truths.

From the same ghazal:

Couplet:
Apnī ḳhushī se jaao to jaate nahīñ kahīñ,
jaane kahāñ kahāñ liye be-ḳhudī chale.
(If we were to depart by our own will, we would go nowhere; who knows where we are led, lost in our own heedlessness.)

Couplet:
Daftar mein apnī shaayr-e-ġham kā hai ye hisāb,
aayā na ek pal na ga.ī ek ghaḌī chale.
(In the ledger of this poet of sorrow, this is the reckoning: not a single moment arrived, nor did a single hour pass idly.)

Kise tag karoge jo yeh dard samajhta ho?
